summary: This document defines a way to convey vendor-specific constraints in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP), so a client can ask for path computation using constraints that only certain vendors define, without a new protocol extension each time.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a company has its own special rules for choosing a route. This lets those rules ride along in the question sent to the route planner.

questions: how to add custom constraints to pcep
what is the pcep vendor information object
how do vendors add custom constraints to pcep
what is an enterprise number in pcep
subtitle: A standard container for carrying a vendor's own constraints and metrics inside PCEP messages.

tldr.problem: PCEP can carry standard constraints and metrics, but it has no way to carry vendor-specific metrics or other complex proprietary information in path computation requests.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a VENDOR-INFORMATION object and a VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV. Both hold a 32-bit Enterprise Number that names the vendor, followed by vendor-defined data.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7150 with two changes: the TLV may be used in any PCEP object that supports TLVs, and the object gets a different code point. RFC 7470 has since been updated by RFC 9752.

today: RFC 7470 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7150. It has been updated by RFC 9752.

sections.title: The Gap Being Filled
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a network path using a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks it to do so over PCEP. Requests carry endpoints and may carry simple constraints such as bandwidth and metric maxima. The PCC can also name an objective function with an Objective Function object.

Implementations may offer proprietary objective functions using codepoints reserved for private use. Those functions may need non-standard constraints or metrics, yet the METRIC object only supports standardized metrics, and PCEP has no mechanism for carrying other complex vendor-specific information. This document supplies one: the Vendor Information object, and the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV for use inside any PCEP object that supports TLVs.

Vendor-specific information implies an inability to interoperate at a functional level with other vendors unless they cooperate. Vendors are encouraged to document what their information means and, where there is wider interest, to bring it to the IETF for standardization.
sections.eli5: The route planner understands a fixed list of questions. This adds a blank space where a company can write its own extra question.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 7150
sections.content:
RFC 7470 obsoletes RFC 7150 and makes two changes. First, it clarifies that the TLV is available in any existing or future PCEP object that supports TLVs. Second, it allocates a different code point for the VENDOR-INFORMATION object.

The code point change was needed because of an inadvertent clash with code points used in an Internet-Draft that had been deployed without IANA allocation. The PCE working group surveyed implementations and deployments of RFC 7150 and considers the change safe and not harmful to early implementers.
sections.eli5: Two people had picked the same locker number by accident, so one of them was moved to a new locker.

sections.title: Using the Vendor Information Object
sections.content:
A PCC puts a Vendor Information object in a PCReq message to convey proprietary constraints or metrics. The PCE looks at the Enterprise Number to decide how to interpret it, and must act according to the P flag in the object header. If P is set, the object is mandatory: the request is processed using it or rejected as defined in RFC 5440. If P is clear, the PCE may use or ignore it.

If the PCE supports the object but not the Enterprise Number, and P is set, it MUST reject the PCReq by sending an Error message with Error-Type "Not supported Object" along with the corresponding Vendor Information object.

The object is OPTIONAL in a PCReq. Multiple instances MAY appear in one message, each treated by its own P bit and possibly with different Enterprise Numbers. It can apply to a single request or to a set of synchronized requests, mirroring the Objective Function object. In a PCRep it can be included like any other object. The RFC gives the message encodings in Routing Backus-Naur Form, adding a vendor-info-list in several positions of the request and response.
sections.eli5: The note has a sticker that says either "you must read this" or "read it if you like". If the planner cannot read the company's code and the sticker says must, it sends the request back.

sections.title: Older Implementations
sections.content:
A legacy implementation that does not recognize the Vendor Information object follows RFC 5440. If the P flag is set, the message is rejected with a PCErr message of Error Type 3 ("Unknown Object"). If P is not set, the object can safely be ignored.

For the TLV, an implementation that does not recognize it follows RFC 5440, where unrecognized TLVs MUST be ignored. A PCE that does support the TLV but does not know the Enterprise Number MUST treat it as an unknown TLV. The RFC adds that further specifications are needed to define the position and meaning of the TLV in specific PCEP objects.
sections.eli5: If the planner has never heard of vendor notes at all, it either refuses a must-read note or quietly skips an optional one.

sections.title: The Object and TLV Format
sections.content:
The object and the TLV share one body format and follow the general PCEP object and TLV formats of RFC 5440. The identifiers are Object-Class 34, Object-Type 1, and TLV Type 7.

The body has an Enterprise Number, a 32-bit integer that uniquely identifies an organization and is assigned by IANA, followed by Enterprise-Specific Information. The format and meaning of the latter belong to the enterprise. They may be published, for example in an Informational RFC or commercial documentation, so that outsiders can use them.
sections.eli5: The envelope has the company's ID number on the front and whatever the company wants to say inside.

sections.title: Management and Operations
sections.content:
A PCC that uses vendor information MAY make it configurable across the whole PCC, per PCE, or per request. A PCE MAY make support configurable and allow policies for its use. The RFC says standard MIB modules should NOT be extended to carry detailed vendor content, though they MAY be extended to report use of the object or TLV and the Enterprise Numbers seen.

Extra vendor data can congest PCEP if the PCE does not support it, so a PCC SHOULD monitor PCE capabilities and SHOULD NOT send vendor information to a PCE it believes does not support it and will not forward the request to one that does. Advertising supported Enterprise Numbers, for instance through PCE discovery, is suggested but out of scope.
sections.eli5: Do not send a note in a secret code to a planner that cannot read it. It only clogs the mailbox.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extensions do not substantially change PCEP, so the security considerations of RFC 5440 apply unchanged. The RFC notes that an attacker might make PCEP messages as large as possible to consume bandwidth and processing power, and that the object and TLV could be a vector for this. The authentication and integrity procedures of RFC 5440 can protect against it.
sections.eli5: Someone could stuff the envelope with junk to slow things down, so the usual protections still matter.

fields.name: Enterprise Number
fields.desc: IANA-assigned identifier of the organization that defines the content.
